title: Apartment Building Lifespan: When Must It Be Demolished? (2026)
desc: How long an apartment building can be used, what happens at expiry, the 5 demolition cases, who inspects, and owners' resettlement rights (Housing Law 2023).
summary: How the service life of an apartment building is determined, the cases requiring demolition and owners' rights in renovation or rebuilding under the Housing Law 2023.
body: p

Apartment buyers often worry that "an apartment can only be lived in for 50 years". In fact, the Housing Law 2023 does not fix a single figure but ties the service life to the design dossier and the actual quality inspection result.
h2
1. How is an apartment building's service life determined?
p
Under Article 58 of the Housing Law:
ul
The service life is determined by the design dossier and the actual period of use according to the inspection conclusion of the competent authority.
The design service life must be stated clearly in the appraisal document of the competent construction authority.
The term is counted from acceptance of the apartment building for use.
p
The apartment sale contract must also state the service life of the apartment building under the design dossier (Clause 2, Article 163). Buyers should read this clause carefully before signing.
h2
2. What happens at expiry?
p

When an apartment building reaches the end of its design life, or has not yet reached it but is damaged, at risk of collapse or unsafe, the provincial People's Committee must direct inspection and quality assessment (Clause 3, Article 58; Article 61). The inspection conclusion must state clearly whether the building must be demolished; if not, it states the period it may continue to be used, and is published on the website of the provincial housing management authority.
p
In other words, reaching the end of the design life does not automatically lead to demolition; a building that is still safe may continue to be used as stated in the inspection conclusion.
h2
3. Cases in which an apartment building must be demolished
p
Under Clause 2, Article 59 of the Housing Law, an apartment building (whether or not past its service life) must be demolished when:
ol
It is damaged by fire or explosion and no longer meets safety conditions for continued use.
It is damaged by natural disaster or war and no longer meets safety conditions.
The main load-bearing structure is dangerous as a whole, at risk of collapse, requiring urgent relocation.

There is severe damage with localised danger to the main load-bearing structure, and the fire protection, water supply and drainage, wastewater treatment, power supply or internal traffic systems do not meet standards or risk being unsafe.

One of the main structures (foundation, column, wall, beam, girder) is damaged and the building lies in an area that must be renovated or rebuilt in coordination with an apartment building that must be demolished under the plan.
h2
4. Apartment owners' rights in renovation or rebuilding
p
Under Article 60 of the Housing Law:
ul
Renovation or rebuilding must be carried out under a project, in conformity with the zoning plan and the province's plan for renovating and rebuilding apartment buildings.
If the plan still allows an apartment building to be rebuilt, the owner is entitled to on-site resettlement, unless they do not want it.
If the apartment building is not rebuilt, the owner is entitled to cash compensation or resettlement elsewhere, with priority given to the same commune-level area.
If a building is demolished due to fire, explosion or natural disaster and is not yet in the plan, the provincial People's Committee must arrange temporary accommodation and relocate residents.
p
Maintenance funds for the apartment building not used up at demolition are used to support resettlement or transferred to the maintenance fund of the new building (Clause 1, Article 155).
h2
5. Who demolishes, and how?
p

After relocation is complete, the project investor for the renovation or rebuilding organises demolition under a plan appraised and approved by the provincial housing management authority within 30 days. Where urgent demolition is needed to ensure the safety of surrounding works, the provincial housing management authority prepares the plan and submits it to the provincial People's Committee for decision (Article 75).
p
For detached houses, the cases requiring demolition are provided separately in Article 136 of the Housing Law.
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. The Housing Law 2023 is currently partially no longer in effect and some articles still refer to the "district level" under the former government model. The inspection procedure follows construction law. To find out whether your apartment building already has an inspection conclusion, ask the Department of Construction where the building is located.
